extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century reading public interested in manners, literature, religion, and theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging satirical/moral essays on manners and religion — what topics and tones are proper, and how satire should discriminate between corrigible faults and undeserving targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in self-presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Call upon Mankind to value and esteem those who set a moderate Price upon their own Merit; keep your Desires, your Words and Actions, within the Regard you observe your Friends have for you; and never, if it were in a Man's Power, to take as much as he possibly might either in Preferment or Reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrogance or taking more than one's deserts causes people to reassess and reduce their esteem (a 'Commission of Bankruptcy upon him'); habitual pretension will make civility and praise fall short of what the person expects. Example: public airs, ostentation, and taking credit one cannot sustain lead to loss of reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-denial / modesty as a practical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-denial is frequently attended with unexpected Blessings, which in the End abundantly recompense such Losses as the Modest seem to suffer in the ordinary Occurrences of Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty reduces ambition and anxieties ('the very Contrary of Ambition'); it increases enjoyment (doubles the pleasures of life), preserves health from care, removes emulation, and makes one 'every Man's Well-wisher.' In adversity, one who acted with gentleness gains pity and unenvied honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model qualities of the modest man (Lucceius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucceius has Learning, Wit, Humour, Eloquence, but no ambitious Prospects to pursue with these Advantages; he wants no Man's Admiration, is in no Need of Pomp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical markers: contentment with simple fashions and warm clothes, companions judged by civility and good nature rather than rank, no superfluous display at meals or in company, lack of prejudice and mastery of appetite — these habits make life easy and agreeable in all places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer Rule 1 — pray for what is truly good; submit to divine will
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a short, comprehensive petition: 'O Jupiter, give us those Things which are good for us, whether they are such Things as we pray for, or such Things as we do not pray for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pray blindly for apparent blessings (e.g., sovereignty) since consequences unknown to us may turn them into curses. The most humble/prudent prayer is to ask that God's will be done ('not my Will, but thine be done'), trusting divine wisdom about what is truly beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer Rule 2 — cultivate wisdom to know what to ask for
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary to apply oneself to the Study of true Wisdom, and to the Knowledge of that which is his chief Good, so that one may ask such Things as are expedient for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without knowledge of the chief good, petitioners are apt to request what is harmful. Education in virtue and wisdom is a precondition for making prayer effective and prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer Rule 3 — live a life of duty to make prayers acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Method to draw down Blessings and render Prayers acceptable is to live in a constant Practice of Duty towards the Gods and towards Men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lacedemonians' form of prayer ('give us all good Things so long as they were virtuous') pleased the gods because it implied virtue; sacrifices and offerings without sincere virtue are like bribes and not acceptable—moral conduct makes devotions efficacious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal worship: conformity in psalm-singing
rubrics_metrics.description: Singing the Psalms in a different Tune from the rest of the Congregation, is a Sort of Schism not tolerated by that Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a fashionable widow introducing Italian airs and divisions into the hundredth Psalm disrupts congregational devotion, makes the parish ridiculous, and spreads the 'infection' (others copying her). Practical rule: do not sing in a different key or introduce operatic ornamentation during communal worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical/audience etiquette — appropriate emotional response
rubrics_metrics.description: The Appetites are sooner moved than the Passions: a sly bawdy expression makes an audience smirk while a sentence describing inward sentiment is often received with coldness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences ought to respond with suitable emotions (pity at moving tragic incidents rather than laughter). The essay laments levity and impertinence in audiences who laugh at tragic astonishment or at a criminal being stabbed; recommends preserving 'Pity' and the capacity to be sensibly touched by serious art. Social pressures (ridicule by companions) inhibit proper responses like tears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: expose corrigible faults and discriminate targets
rubrics_metrics.description: A Satyr should expose nothing but what is corrigible, and make a due Discrimination between those who are, and those who are not the proper Objects of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid levelling satire that censures the whole species (e.g., broad attacks by Juvenal or Boileau); such universal denunciation is useless. Effective satire should single out faults that can be corrected and distinguish between vicious and virtuous members of a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency / bienséance in allusion and translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule of observing what the French call the bienséance, in an Allusion, has been found out of later Years; the ancients provided likeness in similitudes without much care for decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating or alluding, respect modern decency and the capacity of the language: avoid reproducing indecent comparisons when the target language or audience will find them offensive. Simonides' satyr contains coarse touches suited to his age, but modern writers should discriminate and avoid offending tastes.
